summary: In WAL mode, SQLite appends committed pages to the -wal file. A checkpoint copies those pages back into the main database file so the WAL can be rewound and reused. By default SQLite runs a PASSIVE auto-checkpoint when a commit leaves the WAL at 1000 pages or more, and once more when the last connection closes. Applications can run checkpoints themselves through sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() or PRAGMA wal_checkpoint. There are four modes: PASSIVE, FULL, RESTART and TRUNCATE. A checkpoint cannot move past the snapshot of any open reader. If there is always at least one reader, the WAL never resets and grows without bound; this is called checkpoint starvation. A checkpoint does not shrink the WAL file unless TRUNCATE mode or journal_size_limit is used. Checkpointing decides how large the WAL gets, how fast reads are, how much latency writes see, and where fsync happens. Tools such as Litestream take over checkpointing themselves.

claims.text: A checkpoint moves the transactions in the WAL file back into the main database file. SQLite runs one automatically when a COMMIT leaves the WAL at 1000 pages or more (about 4 MB with the default page size), and when the last connection to the database closes. The compile-time option SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT changes the 1000-page default.

PRAGMA wal_autocheckpoint=N, or the sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint() C function, sets the auto-checkpoint threshold in pages. Setting N to zero or a negative value turns auto-checkpointing off. Every automatic checkpoint runs in PASSIVE mode.
SQLite builds the auto-checkpoint on top of sqlite3_wal_hook(). An application can register its own wal_hook, which runs on every commit, and call sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() based on its own rules.

PASSIVE mode copies as many frames as it can without waiting for readers or writers. It never calls the busy handler, and it may leave the checkpoint unfinished. FULL mode calls the busy handler and waits until there is no writer and every reader is on the latest snapshot. It then copies all frames, and it blocks new writers while it waits. RESTART does what FULL does, then also waits until no reader is using the WAL, so the next writer starts the WAL from the beginning. TRUNCATE does what RESTART does, then truncates the WAL file to zero bytes just before it returns successfully.
NOOP mode copies no frames. Its only use is to read the WAL size (*pnLog) and the number of frames already checkpointed (*pnCkpt). After a successful TRUNCATE, both values are 0.

PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(MODE) returns one row with three columns. The first is busy: 0 means SQLITE_OK, and 1 means a FULL, RESTART or TRUNCATE checkpoint was blocked from finishing. The second is the number of pages in the WAL. The third is the number of pages moved back into the database file. If the database is not in WAL mode, the second and third columns are -1. With no argument, the pragma is the same as calling sqlite3_wal_checkpoint(), which runs a PASSIVE checkpoint.

Every checkpoint takes an exclusive checkpoint lock. If another connection is already checkpointing, the call returns SQLITE_BUSY at once and does not call the busy handler. In FULL, RESTART and TRUNCATE modes, if the busy handler gives up while waiting for the writer lock or for readers, the checkpoint continues as a PASSIVE one and returns SQLITE_BUSY. In that case TRUNCATE does not shrink the WAL file.

A checkpoint must stop at the first WAL frame that is newer than the end mark of any current reader. It records its progress in the wal-index and continues from there on the next call. As a result, one long-running read transaction can stop all checkpoint progress.

Checkpoint starvation: if there is always at least one overlapping reader, no checkpoint completes and the WAL file grows without bound. SQLite recommends leaving 'reader gaps' with no readers and running checkpoints during them, or running RESTART or TRUNCATE checkpoints, which can make readers wait.

Syncthing v2 hit checkpoint starvation in production while processing large folders. Its timer-based application checkpointer could find no window without an active reader, so the WAL could reach multiple gigabytes. The maintainers proposed running the checkpoint heuristic whenever a connection is returned to the pool. As of the 2026-02-06 thread, no fix was confirmed.

A normal checkpoint does not shrink the WAL file. Instead, the next writer rewinds the WAL and overwrites it from the start, because overwriting is faster than appending. Only TRUNCATE mode, or a journal_size_limit setting (default -1, meaning no limit; 0 means always truncate to the minimum size), shrinks the -wal file on disk. journal_size_limit must be set separately for each attached database.

The WAL cannot be reset during a write transaction, so a very large transaction produces an equally large WAL. SQLite checkpoints that WAL only after the transaction commits, and only if no reader blocks it. Since SQLite 3.11.0, the WAL for a single transaction should be roughly proportional to the size of that transaction. For transactions larger than about 100 MB, SQLite says rollback-journal modes are probably faster.

Before a checkpoint copies content, it syncs the WAL. Before it resets the WAL, it syncs the database file. It also needs more seeks than a commit, so a checkpoint is slower than a write transaction. By default, the commit that pushes the WAL over the threshold runs the checkpoint on its own thread, so that occasional commit is much slower than the rest.

With PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL in WAL mode, the checkpoint is the only operation that calls fsync. If a separate thread or process runs the checkpoints, the main thread never blocks on fsync. The cost is that recent commits are not durable and may roll back after a power loss.

Disabling auto-checkpoint without running checkpoints yourself lets the WAL grow without limit. A large WAL also slows reads, so SQLite recommends checkpointing at regular intervals. Frequent checkpoints favour read speed; infrequent checkpoints spread the checkpoint cost over more writes and favour write throughput.
Litestream keeps a long-running read transaction open so that no other process can checkpoint and restart the WAL. Litestream then runs the checkpoints itself, after it has copied the new WAL pages.

Litestream v0.5.x runs checkpoints in three tiers. First, if the WAL passes truncate-page-n (default 121359 pages, about 500 MB), it tries a PASSIVE checkpoint and forces a blocking TRUNCATE only if the WAL is still over the threshold. That passive-first behaviour arrived in v0.5.15. Second, it runs non-blocking PASSIVE checkpoints at min-checkpoint-page-count (default 1000 pages, about 4 MB). Third, it runs time-based checkpoints every checkpoint-interval (default 1m). For applications with long-lived read transactions, the guide recommends truncate-page-n: 0 together with disk-space monitoring, because TRUNCATE blocks writes until all readers finish.

When the last connection to a database closes cleanly, it runs a final checkpoint and then deletes the -wal and -shm files. If the last process exits without closing its connection, or SQLITE_FCNTL_PERSIST_WAL is set, the WAL file stays on disk. The only safe way to remove it is to open the database with sqlite3_open() and close it again.

SQLite fixed a WAL-reset bug in 3.51.3 (2026-03-13). The bug required WAL mode with two or more connections on the same file in separate threads or processes, both trying to write or checkpoint at the same instant.

sources.title: Syncthing forum: Dealing with checkpoint starvation

disagreements.text: The SQLite docs present RESTART and TRUNCATE checkpoints as the remedy for checkpoint starvation and accept that readers may wait. Litestream's guide warns that a blocking TRUNCATE stalls writes behind long-lived readers, and recommends disabling forced truncation (truncate-page-n: 0) for those workloads.

The docs are not consistent about whether RESTART blocks readers. The sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2 page says RESTART 'does not impede readers' and only waits for them. The wal.html page says 'readers might block while the checkpoint is running' under RESTART or TRUNCATE.

open_questions: An unofficial search snippet gave Litestream's default checkpoint trigger as 10 MB. The current official guide says min-checkpoint-page-count is 1000 pages (about 4 MB) and the emergency threshold is about 500 MB. Defaults from older versions such as v0.3.x were not checked.
No primary source quantified how much read speed drops as the WAL grows. wal.html says only that a large WAL hurts read performance.
Not researched: whether wal2 mode (a separate SQLite branch with two alternating WAL files) has reached a mainline release and removes checkpoint starvation.
